title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that evaluated whether inserting an executable emulator validator and a bounded repair policy (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures relative to an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using a deterministic shared-generation paired design, we generated one candidate per task with gpt-5-mini and evaluated that same candidate under both conditions across N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 per topology class). A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) enforced structured workflow policies and could request ≤1 repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces record repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We (1) present concise, literature-grounded positioning and a nearest-work comparison; (2) provide a compact formal definition of the binary outcome used for the confirmatory test and a concrete example from archived scoring artifacts; (3) explain why the shared-generation choice yields high internal validity but can produce a statistical ceiling when generator outputs are uniformly valid; and (4) give artifact-grounded recommendations for future confirmatory designs to exercise repair behavior.

sections.introduction:
LLMs can translate operator intent into concrete configuration commands, promising NetOps productivity gains. However, syntactically plausible outputs may violate workflow invariants (for example, ordering or availability constraints) and only reveal semantic failures in closed-loop execution. Prior work therefore advocates tool-augmented pipelines that validate or emulate generated candidates before enactment. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) to isolate the marginal effect of an executable validator plus a bounded repair policy on identical generator outputs. Research question: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow?

We selected a shared-generation paired design: for each intent→configuration task we produced a single generator candidate (gpt-5-mini) and evaluated that candidate under baseline (LLM-only) and guarded (validator±repair) conditions. This design removes generator variability across paired episodes, isolating validator/repair effects. The trade-off is explicit: if the generator produces uniformly valid candidates for the chosen task set, the validator will never apply repairs and the confirmatory test can be degenerate (a ceiling). The preregistration anticipated this risk and specified sensitivity analyses and exploratory perturbations for future runs.
sections.related_work:
Executable, closed-loop benchmarks and verification tools have shown that text-level correctness alone is insufficient for safe enactment: emulation reveals ordering, availability, and stateful failure modes that syntactic checks miss. Representative recent artifacts include executable NetOps benchmarks and verification/digital-twin architectures that exercise generated changes in emulators (e.g., NetConfArena and related executable-benchmark work). Complementary literature proposes guarded, tool-augmented agent architectures (veto layers, canary enactors, translation-to-formal-model) and generate→validate→repair workflows to mitigate semantic failures.

Nearest-work comparison. Table 1 (compact matrix) highlights core experimental design contrasts with four closest works: NetConfArena (closed-loop emulation benchmark), Benchmarking LLM-Driven Network Configuration Repair (LLM repair/benchmark study), MeshAgent (reliability-oriented LLM-for-NetOps prototype), and Lightyear/Heracles-style verification tools (formal/emulator emphasis). Key differentiators marked are: (a) whether the prior study used closed-loop emulation vs static checks; (b) whether generator variance was isolated (shared vs independent generation); (c) repair budget and policy; (d) task corpus provenance (synthetic/testbed vs production-rooted). Our study differs by using a shared-initial-candidate paired design that holds the generator fixed, an executable emulator validator, and a bounded (≤1) repair budget applied only when validator-detected violations occur. These differences determine what marginal questions each study answers: generator-focused vs validator-focused evaluation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The study was preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) prior to execution. Design: paired-binary confirmatory test with exactly N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks deterministically partitioned into three topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine; 40 tasks each). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Primary test: exact two-sided McNemar; CI: bootstrap-percentile (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The execution contract limited repairs to ≤1 per guarded episode and enforced deterministic emulator resets and contamination checks.

Task payloads and validator semantics. Each task manifest (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) includes initial_state, expected_final_state, a natural-language intent, and an explicit required_sequence describing canonical ordered operations (e.g., shut→configure→restore; make-before-break). The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) implemented as an executable emulator that enforces structured workflow policies derived from the task_payload (examples: must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, minimum_active_in_groups). The validator emits a structured validator_trace with fields validation_before, validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and repair_applied.

Formal binary outcome definition (pass/fail). The confirmatory binary label used in the McNemar test is produced deterministically by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 using scoring_rule = "full_intent_constraint_validation" (scorer_version = 5.0). Decision logic (exact):
- PASS if validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true AND validator_trace.violation_count == 0 AND normalized_response == normalized_reference_answer; otherwise FAIL. Tie-breaks: any terminal_error_type or unscorable parse yields FAIL. Repair invocation: if violation_count>0 and repair budget remains, the guarded policy issues a single repair prompt and revalidates; the final label reflects post-repair validation.

Concrete example from archived artifacts. Task task-000001 scoring artifact (execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json) shows normalized_response == normalized_reference_answer and validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true with violation_count = 0 ⇒ PASS. The same shared-initial candidate appears in both baseline and guarded episodes for pair-000001 and yields PASS in both conditions.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The run completed per preregistration: planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; complete_pair_count = 120; model_calls_used = 120 (one shared initial generation per pair); maximum_model_calls planned = 240; start/completion timestamps recorded in the execution manifest. Contamination checks and deterministic reconciliation passed (provider-call audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 120; cross-condition cache reuse = false). No technical exclusions occurred; analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120.

Primary outcome. Condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) record baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0; guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0 (success rates = 1.0 for both). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p-value = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces record repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes; thus no repair_provider_trace artifacts were generated.

Per-topology counts (representative scoring artifacts). The deterministic partition produced 40 tasks per topology class; per-topology results are: Edge 40/40 baseline and guarded success; Core 40/40 baseline and guarded success; Leaf–spine 40/40 baseline and guarded success. Representative scoring artifacts (for example: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and -guarded.json) show parsed_command_count matching required_command_count and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true.

Statistical interpretation. The paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair marginal effects on identical candidates. However, because the generator outputs in this task bank uniformly satisfied the structured validator, the guard was never exercised and the confirmatory test is degenerate: zero discordant pairs produce a degenerate bootstrap CI (lower==upper==observed difference). This degenerate result is a correct statistical reflection of the observed data under the preregistered test and resampling scheme.
sections.discussion:
Why the ceiling occurred and what it means. The shared-generation design intentionally isolates validator/repair effects by removing generator variance. If the chosen generator/prompt and task bank yield mostly valid candidates, repairs will not be required and the guarded pipeline cannot reduce semantic failures relative to baseline—this is precisely what we observed. The result therefore does not imply that validators are unnecessary in general; instead it documents that, for this curated synthetic corpus under the frozen prompt strategy and model (gpt-5-mini), the generator produced correct enactable candidates.

Design implications and artifact-grounded recommendations. Artifact evidence (task_manifest difficulty metadata and validator_trace summaries) supports four preregistered modifications to increase power to detect repair utility in future confirmatory runs: (1) allow independent per-condition generation (remove shared-generation for a subset) so guards can intercept generator errors; (2) prespecify controlled prompt perturbations on a fraction of tasks to increase generator error incidence while preserving some paired blocks; (3) stratify confirmatory sampling on manifest difficulty labels (e.g., require dependency_rule_count ≥ 2 or tasks labeled 'very_hard'); and (4) relax repair budget in exploratory arms (allow multiple repair iterations) to measure repair convergence and cost. These suggestions map directly to fields and thresholds present in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and require no new instrumentation beyond the archived harness.

Validator encoding and auditability. The emulator validator encodes workflow policies as structured checks drawn from task_payload keys (must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, minimum_active_in_groups). Validator traces show which rules were checked, which fields were touched, and why repairs were not applied. Even when idle, such traces provide operator-facing auditability and third-party inspection capability—an operational value independent of immediate repair activity. Limitations of that encoding are real: validator fidelity is bounded by the task-policy vocabulary and the emulator's model of vendor behavior and observability.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered artifact-rich paired experiment isolating the marginal effect of an executable validator and a bounded repair policy on identical LLM-generated candidates. Observed outcome: all 120 shared candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, producing identical 100% success in baseline and guarded conditions (n_11=120; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference = 0.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00]). The principal scientific contribution is methodological: we show how a preregistered paired design with deterministic archival artifacts cleanly isolates validator effects and supports reproducible auditing, and we document concrete, artifact-grounded adjustments (independent generation, perturbations, difficulty stratification, expanded repair budgets) necessary for future confirmatory studies that aim to measure repair utility when generators more frequently produce invalid candidates.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
